title: What is the MERGE statement and why can it be dangerous?
description: Upserts in one statement: syntax shape, the concurrency race Microsoft documented, and safer upsert patterns for production.

data.text: **Question:** What is the MERGE statement and why can it be dangerous?

`MERGE` (upsert) atomically **inserts, updates, or deletes** target rows based on matching a source against a `WHEN MATCHED` / `WHEN NOT MATCHED` / `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET` structure — the standard tool for synchronizing staging tables into live tables in one statement. It's 'dangerous' for real reasons: under **concurrency**, two simultaneous MERGEs matching nothing can both try to insert the same key (one succeeds, one gets a duplicate-key error — the race documented in KB2470992); it has surprising semantics (multiple MATCHED actions allowed since 2022, target-locking behavior, trigger-ordering rules); and long MERGEs hold bigger lock footprints than the equivalent explicit statements. Production guidance: treat MERGE as useful for **controlled, single-writer ETL**, and prefer an **explicit UPDATE-then-INSERT pattern** (or INSERT with a unique constraint + catch) for concurrent OLTP upserts.

**Syntax shape:**
- `MERGE [TOP(n)] INTO target USING source ON <join condition>`
- `WHEN MATCHED [AND <cond>] THEN UPDATE SET ...` (optionally DELETE since 2022)
- `WHEN NOT MATCHED [BY TARGET] [AND <cond>] THEN INSERT (cols) VALUES (...)`
- `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE [AND <cond>] THEN DELETE/UPDATE` — target rows with no source
- `OUTPUT $action, inserted.*, deleted.*;` — audit what happened
- Must end with a semicolon — a MERGE without one can attach the following statement's INTO and fail confusingly

**The concurrency race (the main 'why dangerous'):**
- Two sessions both run MERGE for key 42; neither finds it (MATCHED = false for both)
- Both take the not-matched path and insert — one wins, the other raises 2601/2627 duplicate key
- Worse pre-fix versions had broader plan bugs; KB2470992 recommends a HOLDLOCK hint (`MERGE INTO t WITH (HOLDLOCK)`) or the explicit two-step pattern to serialize
- Correct OLTP pattern: `UPDATE ...; IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0 BEGIN TRY INSERT ... END TRY BEGIN CATCH IF error_number() IN (2601, 2627) UPDATE ... END CATCH` — or simply attempt INSERT first, fall back to UPDATE on duplicate key

**Other sharp edges:**
- **Locking**: MERGE can lock more of the target than the minimal two-step path — throughput impact on hot tables
- **Triggers**: MERGE fires triggers per row with special semantics; DML triggers on target see combined effects — historically buggy area
- **Multiple WHEN MATCHED clauses** (SQL 2022+): conditions evaluated in order — clever but easy to misread
- **NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE** deleting rows the source merely didn't include — a full-table sync wiping filtered-out rows is a classic incident
- **Semi-hot targeting**: hints, snapshot isolation, and replaying failed batches all behave subtly with MERGE

**When MERGE is fine:**
- Single-threaded ETL staging → fact loads, where the source is the complete truth and one process owns the job
- Bulk synchronization where statement-level atomicity and one round trip matter more than row-level contention

data.title: A staging sync with MERGE — and the safe OLTP alternative
data.code:
-- ETL pattern: sync staging into dim table (single writer)
MERGE dbo.ProductDim AS target
USING dbo.ProductStaging AS source
    ON target.Sku = source.Sku
WHEN MATCHED AND (target.Price <> source.Price
                  OR target.Name <> source.Name) THEN
    UPDATE SET Name = source.Name, Price = source.Price,
               ModifiedAt = SYSDATETIME()
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (Sku, Name, Price, CreatedAt)
    VALUES (source.Sku, source.Name, source.Price, SYSDATETIME());
-- Note the terminating semicolon (required)
OUTPUT $action, inserted.Sku, deleted.Price AS OldPrice;
-- ⚠️ No NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE clause here on purpose:
--   adding THEN DELETE would wipe dim rows absent from staging.

-- ❌ Concurrent OLTP upsert with MERGE: two sessions, key 42 missing in both
--    -> both insert -> duplicate key error 2627 for one session.

-- ✅ Safer OLTP upsert: update first, insert on miss (unique key enforces truth)
UPDATE dbo.Cart SET Qty = @qty, UpdatedAt = SYSDATETIME()
WHERE SessionId = @sid AND ProductId = @pid;

IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0
BEGIN
    BEGIN TRY
        INSERT INTO dbo.Cart (SessionId, ProductId, Qty)
        VALUES (@sid, @pid, @qty);
    END TRY
    BEGIN CATCH
        IF ERROR_NUMBER() IN (2601, 2627)   -- lost the insert race
        BEGIN
            UPDATE dbo.Cart SET Qty = @qty, UpdatedAt = SYSDATETIME()
            WHERE SessionId = @sid AND ProductId = @pid;
        END
        ELSE THROW;
    END CATCH
END
-- Or: MERGE WITH (HOLDLOCK) if you must keep one statement under concurrency.

data.title: The clause people add by reflex
data.text: WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE turns a 'sync what's in staging' into 'delete everything that isn't' — on a dim table fed by a partial extract, that silently deletes history. Make deletions explicit and conditional (a status column), never a default clause.

Interviewers want to assess:
- Knowing MERGE's three-way structure and $action auditing
- Awareness of the documented concurrency race and its mitigation (HOLDLOCK / two-step)
- The NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE deletion hazard
- Judgment: MERGE for single-writer ETL, explicit upserts for concurrent OLTP

items: Using MERGE for high-concurrency upserts without HOLDLOCK — duplicate-key races
Adding NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE with a partial source — mass unintended deletes
MERGE on hot OLTP tables where its lock footprint exceeds the two-step alternative
Not using OUTPUT $action to audit what the sync actually did
Assuming trigger behavior on MERGE is identical to plain INSERT/UPDATE
Walk through the double-insert race under default isolation
How does the 2022 multi-clause WHEN MATCHED change the semantics?
How would you make a partial sync safe for a slowly-changing dimension?
When is INSERT...ON DUPLICATE-style logic (via catch) genuinely better than MERGE?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: MERGE: one statement for insert/update/delete-by-match, with $action output
Concurrency race: two sessions both not-matched → duplicate insert; mitigate or avoid
NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE deletes are the classic sync disaster
Fine for single-writer ETL; prefer explicit UPDATE/INSERT upserts under contention
data.takeaway: MERGE is a power tool: excellent in one writer's hands on a staging load, and the source of some of the most famous production incidents in concurrent OLTP.
